Apple’s guidance indicates that developers should complete the transition by the end of 2026, and users who rely on older Intel‑only applications will need to seek alternative solutions or maintain older macOS installations. The company will continue to provide Rosetta 2 support for a limited period to ease the transition, but the final version of macOS 15 will remove the capability entirely.

In summary, macOS 15 will mark the end of Rosetta’s support for Intel applications, reflecting Apple’s commitment to a fully ARM‑based ecosystem. Users and developers are advised to plan accordingly, ensuring that critical software is updated or replaced before the release to avoid compatibility issues.
author: Ars Technica

title: Unitree Leads Market in Affordable Humanoid Robots Thanks to Founder’s Cost‑Cutting Focus
content:
Wang Xingxing, the former chief operating officer of Unitree Robotics, is credited with steering the Shenzhen‑based startup from a niche robotics lab to a global supplier of autonomous service robots. During his tenure, the company secured more than 30 million dollars in venture funding, expanded its product line to include humanoid, quadruped, and industrial robots, and entered key markets in North America and Europe. Analysts attribute this rapid growth to Wang’s hands‑on approach, noting that he routinely reviewed design schematics, production schedules, and customer feedback, often making last‑minute adjustments that kept the company ahead of competitors.

Wang’s micromanagement style is characterized by daily stand‑ups with engineering teams, detailed oversight of supply‑chain logistics, and a personal involvement in marketing strategy. Under his direction, Unitree’s flagship quadruped robot, the Laikago, achieved a 20% faster development cycle than industry averages, while the company reported a 35% increase in year‑over‑year revenue. However, the same intensity that accelerated product launches has also raised concerns about scalability; internal reports indicate that as the workforce grew from 50 to 200 employees, Wang’s direct involvement in every project phase became increasingly difficult to sustain.

Whether Wang’s approach can be replicated at a larger scale depends on Unitree’s ability to institutionalize his decision‑making processes. The company is reportedly exploring a hybrid model that blends centralized oversight with delegated authority, aiming to preserve the agility that defined its early success while enabling broader operational expansion. The outcome will likely influence how fast‑moving robotics firms balance visionary leadership with the practical demands of scaling.
author: Ars Technica

title: OpenAI Stays in Antitrust Fight with Musk After Apple Settles ChatGPT Deal
content:
Elon Musk has paused his public criticism of Apple after the company’s recent decision to allow ChatGPT to be installed on iOS devices. In a series of tweets last week, Musk accused Apple of stifling competition by refusing to support OpenAI’s flagship language model, calling the move a “strategic blunder.” Following a brief exchange with Apple’s chief technology officer, Musk said he would no longer target the tech giant in his social‑media outbursts, noting that the company’s new policy now permits third‑party AI apps on the App Store.

Despite the truce with Apple, Musk has continued to voice concerns about OpenAI’s business practices. He has highlighted the firm’s rapid growth, its high valuation, and its handling of user data, arguing that OpenAI’s “unregulated” approach could pose risks to consumers and the broader tech ecosystem. Musk’s comments come as OpenAI prepares to launch a new version of ChatGPT and as regulators in several countries begin to scrutinize AI companies’ data‑usage policies.

The shift in Musk’s focus underscores the evolving dynamics between major technology players and the emerging AI sector. While Apple’s decision to open its platform to ChatGPT may ease tensions, Musk’s ongoing scrutiny of OpenAI suggests that the debate over AI governance and corporate responsibility remains far from settled.
author: Ars Technica

title: AI infrastructure firm Cornelis raises $205 million and launches Active Compute Fabric
content:
The company unveiled a new product, Active Compute Fabric, during its latest product launch. The technology is a specialized network solution designed to address a well‑known bottleneck in high‑performance computing: the idle time that GPUs experience while waiting for data to arrive over conventional interconnects.

Active Compute Fabric introduces a low‑latency, high‑bandwidth fabric that aligns data delivery more closely with GPU processing cycles. By reducing the time GPUs spend idling, the system promises to improve throughput for data‑intensive workloads such as machine‑learning training, scientific simulations, and real‑time analytics. The company highlighted that the fabric’s architecture allows for dynamic routing and prioritization of critical data streams, potentially lowering overall system costs by maximizing existing GPU utilization.

If the performance gains claimed by the company materialize in production environments, Active Compute Fabric could become a key component in next‑generation data centers, enabling faster, more efficient processing of large‑scale workloads while mitigating the cost and energy penalties associated with idle GPU cycles.
author: TechCrunch

title: OpenAI acquires Glass Imaging for $300 million
content:
Glass Imaging, a newly launched imaging technology company, was founded by two former Apple engineers who previously headed the team responsible for developing Apple’s Portrait Mode. The startup aims to leverage the duo’s expertise in computational photography to create advanced imaging solutions for a range of devices.

The founders’ experience with Portrait Mode—a feature that uses depth mapping and machine‑learning algorithms to produce studio‑quality portraits on smartphones—provides Glass Imaging with a strong technical foundation. By building on the proprietary techniques honed at Apple, the company intends to offer developers and manufacturers tools that enhance photo quality and depth perception across platforms. Industry observers note that the venture could accelerate the adoption of sophisticated camera capabilities beyond Apple’s ecosystem.
author: TechCrunch

title: Nvidia CEO Huang Opposes AI Slowdown
content:
Elon Musk and Sam Altman have publicly backed Dario Amodei’s recent appeal to slow the pace of artificial‑intelligence development, citing safety and governance concerns. Amodei, the former OpenAI vice‑president and current founder of Anthropic, has warned that rapid progress could outstrip the world’s ability to regulate and mitigate risks. Both Musk and Altman have echoed these cautions in interviews and on social media, urging the industry to adopt more stringent oversight.

In contrast, Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, has expressed a more optimistic view on the speed of AI advancement. Huang has repeatedly highlighted Nvidia’s role in providing the hardware that powers next‑generation models and has suggested that accelerated development can be managed through responsible engineering and collaboration with regulators. He has emphasized the economic and societal benefits of faster AI deployment, arguing that a cautious slowdown could hinder innovation and global competitiveness.

The differing positions underscore a broader debate within the AI community about how best to balance rapid technological progress with safety and ethical considerations. While Amodei, Musk, and Altman call for deliberate pacing and stronger governance frameworks, Huang’s stance reflects a belief that the benefits of swift AI deployment can be realized without compromising safety, provided that appropriate safeguards are in place. The conversation continues as industry leaders and policymakers grapple with how to chart a path forward for the field.
author: TechCrunch

title: US Space Force Confirms Weapons in Orbit
content:
Space, once a stage for Cold‑War prestige, has become a critical arena for national security and technological competition. In recent years, governments worldwide have accelerated investment in orbital capabilities, launching satellites that provide advanced communications, navigation, and intelligence-gathering functions. The shift reflects a broader recognition that control of space assets can translate into strategic advantages on the ground, influencing everything from military operations to economic resilience.

Key developments include the rapid expansion of commercial launch providers, the emergence of reusable launch vehicles, and the growing presence of anti‑satellite weaponry. Several countries have announced plans to develop or acquire systems capable of disabling or destroying adversary satellites, while others are investing in hardened platforms and space debris mitigation. These moves are accompanied by diplomatic efforts to establish norms and treaties that could govern space conduct, though consensus remains elusive amid competing national interests.

The evolving landscape underscores the need for robust policy frameworks and international cooperation. As nations vie for dominance in orbit, the potential for conflict—whether accidental or intentional—intensifies. Ensuring that space remains a domain for peaceful use while safeguarding national security interests will likely shape global security dynamics for the foreseeable future.
author: Euronews

title: Dangote refinery seeks $1.6 billion from African retail investors
content:
Nigeria’s flagship Dangote refinery announced a public‑ownership initiative, seeking to raise roughly $1.6 billion from retail investors throughout Africa. The move aims to broaden participation in the country’s largest oil‑processing facility and to mobilise private capital for further expansion. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, President Félix Tshisekedi appealed to the National Service to undertake a city‑wide clean‑up of Kinshasa’s streets, emphasizing the need for improved sanitation and civic responsibility. Meanwhile, with the Youth Olympic Games only six weeks away, the Olympic flame commenced its symbolic tour of Senegal, the host nation, marking the start of a series of events that will culminate in the opening ceremony.

These developments reflect a broader regional focus on infrastructure investment, public engagement, and international sporting prestige. The Dangote fundraising effort could reshape ownership structures in the West African energy sector, while the Kinshasa clean‑up initiative underscores governmental priorities on urban hygiene. The flame’s journey through Senegal serves both as a promotional platform for the upcoming Games and as a reminder of the continent’s growing role in global athletics.
author: France 24

title: Dangote refinery launches largest African IPO
content:
Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote has initiated the continent’s largest ever share offering, listing 4.1 billion shares of his Lagos refinery on the Nigerian Stock Exchange. Marketed as a “people’s IPO,” the float aims to give ordinary Nigerians an opportunity to invest in the refinery’s projected earnings. The offering is slated to begin trading in November, marking a significant step toward broader public participation in one of Africa’s most valuable energy assets.

The timing coincides with a rise in global oil prices after Yemen’s Houthi rebels attacked Saudi facilities, prompting the shutdown of the kingdom’s East‑West crude pipeline. The supply disruption has heightened market volatility, underscoring the strategic importance of Dangote’s refinery for regional energy security. The new listing is expected to attract both domestic and international investors seeking exposure to Africa’s expanding oil sector.
author: France 24

title: Turkish police raid gay bars, arrest 60 LGBTQ activists
content:
Turkish police conducted coordinated raids on several gay bars and the residences of LGBTQ activists on Sunday, detaining at least 60 individuals, officials said. Authorities described the operation as part of an effort to reinforce “traditional family values,” a stance echoed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who has repeatedly characterized the LGBTQ community as a “deviant movement” of “perverts” and linked it to Turkey’s declining birth rate. The sweeps, which targeted both nightlife venues and private homes, have drawn criticism from human‑rights groups who note a pattern of state‑led harassment against sexual minorities in the country.

In a related interview, FRANCE 24’s Monte Francis spoke with Yildiz Tar, editor‑in‑chief of the LGBTQ platform KaosGL.org, about the impact of the raids and the broader climate of repression. Tar highlighted the community’s concerns over increasing police scrutiny and the chilling effect on activism, while emphasizing the need for international attention to Turkey’s treatment of LGBTQ citizens. The incident underscores ongoing tensions between the government’s cultural policies and the rights of minority groups within the nation.
author: France 24

title: Fact-check shows viral videos misrepresent Houthi attacks, using drill footage and unrelated fire clips
content:
A video circulating on X that purported to depict Houthi rebels ambushing Saudi‑backed mercenaries has attracted millions of views, but the footage has been debunked as unrelated military drills. FRANCE 24 Observers determined that the clip originates from a 2024 Houthi training exercise and was later altered with football commentary and blurred flags. The original flags, which were obscured in the edited version, displayed the emblems of Israel, the United Kingdom and the United States, not those of Saudi Arabia as the post claimed.

Additional viral videos that were linked to recent Houthi attacks on a Saudi Aramco refinery have also been proven false. Investigations traced the alleged attack footage to separate incidents—a fire in Texas and another blaze in Russia—none of which involved Houthi forces. The fact‑check, conducted by Vedika Bahl for Truth or Fake, underscores the prevalence of misattributed content online and highlights the need for careful verification of visual claims in conflict reporting.
author: France 24

title: Israeli rights group says West Bank policies aim to erase Palestinian presence
content:
Israeli human‑rights organization B’Tselem released a report on Monday alleging that a coordinated set of Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank is intended to prevent Palestinians from existing as a unified people. The document, titled “The Elimination Project,” claims the policies constitute a broader strategy rather than isolated incidents.

The report identifies five interlinked tactics: the use of violence, ethnic cleansing, restrictions on movement, economic strangulation, and the systematic destruction of social and political structures. B’Tselem argues that these measures collectively aim to undermine Palestinian society and its capacity for self‑determination. FRANCE 24’s Selina Sykes covered the release, noting that the findings add to ongoing debates over the legality and humanitarian impact of Israeli policies in the territory.
author: France 24

title: Bob Mackie iconic Hollywood designer dies at 87
content:
Hollywood costume designer Bob Mackie, celebrated for creating iconic looks for stars such as Cher and Elton John, died on Monday at the age of 87, his official Instagram account confirmed. The announcement, posted by the designer’s family, marked the end of a five‑decade career that helped define red‑carpet glamour and pop‑culture style.

Mackie’s work spanned theatre, film, and television, and included a high‑profile collaboration with Mattel to design a clothing line for Barbie dolls. His signature sequined gowns and bold silhouettes became synonymous with celebrity fashion throughout the 1970s and beyond. French news outlet France 24, with reporter Camille Knight, provided additional coverage of his life and contributions to the entertainment industry. Mackie’s passing closes a chapter on a prolific career that left an indelible mark on costume design worldwide.
author: France 24

title: US Space Force confirms first deployment of weapons in orbit
content:
The U.S. Space Force announced on Tuesday that the United States has deployed weapons in orbit, marking the first official confirmation of such capabilities. The disclosure comes amid heightened attention to the militarization of space and underscores a shift toward openly acknowledging the presence of offensive and defensive systems beyond Earth’s atmosphere.

The statement arrives as China and Russia also expand their own space‑based military assets, prompting Washington to emphasize the need for control of the space domain and the protection of satellites that support military communications, surveillance and navigation. Officials indicated that the new capabilities are intended to deter potential threats and ensure the resilience of critical space infrastructure, signaling an escalating strategic competition among the three powers.
author: France 24

title: Macklemore removed from Ed Sheeran US tour after pro-Palestinian comment
content:
American rapper Macklemore announced on Monday that he has been removed from Ed Sheeran’s U.S. stadium tour after he shouted “Free Palestine” during a September 4 concert in New Jersey. The Grammy‑winning artist said the decision came after pressure from several venue owners, most notably New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who objected to Macklemore’s criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza.

The tour cancellation highlights the ongoing tension between performers’ political statements and the commercial interests of large‑scale concert venues. While Macklemore’s remarks were made in a live setting, organizers cited concerns over potential backlash and safety issues as the basis for his removal. The incident underscores the broader debate over free expression in the entertainment industry as artists navigate increasingly polarized political climates.
author: France 24

title: EU develops new Arctic strategy amid geopolitical tensions
content:
European policymakers have placed the Arctic at the forefront of their strategic agenda as a confluence of geopolitical pressures intensifies interest in the region. Russia’s expanded military activities in the High North, coupled with former U.S. President Donald Trump’s public statements threatening U.S. claims over Greenland, have heightened security concerns among EU member states. At the same time, the growing demand for critical raw materials such as rare earth elements, lithium and cobalt—essential for renewable‑energy technologies and defense applications—has spurred a competitive race to secure access to Arctic mineral deposits.

In response, the European Union is accelerating diplomatic and research initiatives aimed at strengthening its presence in the Arctic while promoting sustainable development. The EU’s upcoming Arctic policy review will address coordination with NATO allies, investment in responsible mining practices, and collaboration with indigenous communities to balance economic interests with environmental protection. By aligning security, economic, and climate objectives, Europe seeks to safeguard its strategic interests and ensure a stable, cooperative framework for the Arctic’s future.
author: DW World

title: Israel probes Naza Gaza film for treason and anti‑Semitism
content:
A new documentary released this week alleges that the Israeli military routinely incorporates the expectation of mass civilian casualties into its operational planning for the ongoing conflict in Gaza. The film, titled *Collateral Damage: The Hidden Calculus of War*, features interviews with former Israeli defense officials, Palestinian survivors, and independent analysts who claim that strategic decisions are made with an acceptance that large numbers of non‑combatants will be killed. According to the filmmakers, internal documents and testimonies reveal a pattern of targeting densely populated areas, using tactics such as extensive airstrikes and ground incursions that, they argue, prioritize military objectives over civilian protection.

The documentary has sparked debate among international human‑rights groups and governmental bodies. Organizations such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have called for independent investigations into the alleged practices, while Israeli officials have dismissed the film’s claims as unfounded and politically motivated. The release comes amid heightened scrutiny of the war in Gaza, which has resulted in thousands of civilian deaths and widespread destruction, and adds to ongoing discussions about compliance with international humanitarian law and the classification of the conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US blocks Iran nuclear chief's visa for Vienna conference
content:
Tehran has lodged a formal complaint against Washington, accusing the United States of exerting pressure on Austria to cancel the visa of Mohammad Eslami, a senior Iranian official slated to attend a conference in Vienna. Iran’s foreign ministry said the alleged intervention breaches the sovereign rights of an EU member state to determine its own visa policy and constitutes an unwarranted intrusion into the internal affairs of a fellow United Nations member. The statement, issued on Thursday, did not provide evidence of the U.S. lobbying but referenced recent diplomatic exchanges in which American officials expressed concerns over Eslami’s participation due to his role in Iran’s nuclear and missile programs.

Austria’s foreign ministry confirmed that the visa revocation was decided after a review of security considerations, but declined to comment on any external influence. The United States has not responded to the accusation, while European officials have emphasized the autonomy of each member state in handling visa matters. Iran warned that such actions could further strain relations with the West and called for respect of international norms governing diplomatic travel. The episode adds to a series of recent tensions between Tehran and Washington over Iran’s nuclear activities and regional policies.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Talks in Oman between Iran and Gulf Arab states postponed
content:
Hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in the conflict involving Iran and Gulf states were dampened on Monday when the scheduled talks in Muscat were postponed. The meeting, which was to bring together senior officials from Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman, was intended to address the ongoing hostilities that have spilled over from the war in Yemen and heightened tensions across the Gulf region. Organizers cited “logistical constraints” and the need for additional preparation time as the reasons for the delay, though they did not specify which parties requested the postponement.

The postponement comes after months of intermittent negotiations mediated by Oman, which has positioned itself as a neutral facilitator in the dispute. Analysts note that the delay may prolong the stalemate and hinder efforts to de‑escalate the proxy fighting that has caused significant civilian casualties and disrupted maritime trade routes. Both Tehran and the Gulf capitals have reaffirmed their commitment to resume dialogue, but the setback underscores the fragility of the process and the challenges remaining before a comprehensive settlement can be reached.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Former Columbia student Mahmoud Khalil sues university and dean for discrimination
content:
Activist and former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil has filed a civil lawsuit against Columbia University and Dean of the School of General Studies, Dr. Michael Rosenberg. The complaint, lodged in New York State Supreme Court on Tuesday, alleges that the university and the dean engaged in actions that violated Khalil’s constitutional and statutory rights while he was enrolled as a student and later as an activist on campus.

According to the filing, Khalil contends that the defendants’ conduct resulted in personal and professional harm, prompting him to seek monetary damages and injunctive relief. The lawsuit adds that the alleged misconduct reflects broader concerns about the treatment of student activists at higher‑education institutions. Columbia University has not yet issued a public response, and the case is expected to proceed through the standard pre‑trial motions and discovery process.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Macklemore claims he was removed from Ed Sheeran's US tour over pro-Palestinian stance
content:
Macklemore announced that he was removed from Ed Sheeran’s upcoming U.S. tour after the singer’s management cited the rapper’s public support for Palestine as the reason for the decision. The Seattle‑born artist made the claim in a series of social‑media posts on Tuesday, stating that the cancellation occurred despite his contract being finalized and that he was not provided with an official explanation beyond the reference to his “pro‑Palestinian stance.” He added that the removal came just weeks before the tour’s scheduled start in early October.

Ed Sheeran’s representatives have not issued a detailed comment, but a spokesperson for the tour’s production company confirmed that lineup changes were being made for “logistical and artistic considerations.” The incident follows a broader pattern of heightened scrutiny over artists’ political expressions, with several musicians facing similar cancellations or venue restrictions amid the ongoing Israel‑Palestine conflict. As the tour approaches, both parties have indicated that the matter remains unresolved, leaving fans uncertain about the final roster of supporting acts.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US repeals power plant greenhouse gas emission rules
content:
The Trump administration announced that recent regulatory changes could save U.S. power plants more than $300 billion over the next decade and “unleash” American energy production. The estimate, released by the White House Office of Energy and Climate Policy, is based on projected reductions in compliance costs resulting from the rollback of the Obama‑era Clean Power Plan and the easing of emissions reporting requirements for coal, natural‑gas and renewable facilities.

According to the administration, the revised rules will lower operating expenses, reduce the need for costly retrofits, and encourage investment in existing infrastructure, thereby expanding domestic energy capacity. Industry groups have welcomed the move as a boost to competitiveness, while environmental organizations have warned that the cost savings may be offset by increased greenhouse‑gas emissions. The administration plans to finalize the rule changes by the end of the year, positioning the policy as a cornerstone of its broader energy agenda.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israeli strike hits Gaza displacement camp
content:
An Israeli airstrike hit a displacement camp in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing at least several civilians and injuring dozens more, according to reports from local health officials and aid agencies operating in the area. The camp, which shelters families displaced by the ongoing conflict, was struck during a period of intensified hostilities between Israeli forces and Hamas militants. Israeli military spokespersons said the target was a location used by Hamas to launch attacks, while the Palestinian Ministry of Health confirmed the casualties and called for an immediate investigation into the incident.

The strike adds to a growing number of civilian casualties reported in Gaza since the latest round of fighting began, raising renewed concerns from international humanitarian organizations about the protection of non‑combatants in densely populated areas. United Nations officials have urged both sides to adhere to international law and to allow unhindered access for aid delivery. As the situation remains volatile, authorities on both sides have not announced further military actions, and the focus is shifting toward assessing the humanitarian impact of the attack on the displaced population.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Texas landowners sue to halt Trump border wall construction
content:
Indigenous groups, environmental organizations and local residents have voiced strong opposition to the proposed expansion of the U.S.–Mexico border wall in the Big Bend region of Texas. Critics argue that the construction would damage culturally significant sites, disrupt wildlife corridors and threaten the fragile desert ecosystem, while also disregarding the concerns of communities that have lived alongside the border for generations. Federal officials, however, maintain that the barrier is essential for national security and immigration enforcement, citing the need to deter illegal crossings and smuggling activities.

Data from U.S. Customs and Border Protection indicate that the Big Bend sector accounts for roughly one percent of all border-related arrests nationwide, underscoring the relatively low level of illicit activity in the area. The disparity between the projected security benefits and the environmental and cultural costs has intensified the debate, prompting calls for a reassessment of the wall’s necessity in this sparsely trafficked stretch of the border.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Costume designer Bob Mackie dies at 87
content:
Renowned costume designer Bob Mackie, often dubbed the “Sultan of Sequins,” has long been celebrated for his extravagant, glittering creations that have defined the visual identities of several music legends. His work, characterized by bold colors, intricate beadwork and lavish use of sequins, has adorned icons such as Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John, helping to cement their stage personas and contributing to the spectacle of live performance.

Mackie's designs have earned multiple industry accolades and continue to influence contemporary fashion and stagecraft. Recent retrospectives and museum exhibitions have highlighted his contributions, underscoring how his signature sparkle has become synonymous with larger‑than‑life entertainment. As his legacy endures, the “Sultan of Sequins” remains a pivotal figure in the intersection of music, theater and costume design.
author: BBC World

title: SpaceX Wraps Ship 42 Tests, Flight 14 Moves to September 22
content:
SpaceX has finished a multi‑day catch‑related test campaign with its unflown Starship prototype Ship 42 at Pad 2. During the session the company conducted a series of “chopsticks” tests—simulations of the vehicle’s re‑entry and landing sequence—before rolling the ship to a new position for the next phase of evaluation. The tests were designed to verify the vehicle’s ability to decelerate and land safely after a high‑altitude flight.

Following the completion of the catch tests, SpaceX moved Ship 42 to its next test configuration. The company also announced that Flight 14, the upcoming Starship launch that had previously been scheduled for an earlier date, is now slated to go live on the National Evaluation Team’s (NET) September 22 launch window. This shift reflects the company’s ongoing adjustments to its flight schedule as it continues to refine the vehicle’s performance and safety systems.
author: NASASpaceFlight

title: Cygnus the Swan Lifts International Space Station
content:
Local nonprofit **Just a Little Help** announced today that it has secured a new partnership with a group of community supporters, referred to as “its friends,” to expand its outreach programs. The organization, which has been operating in the city for six years, focuses on providing emergency assistance and long‑term support to low‑income families. The partnership will enable the nonprofit to increase its monthly assistance budget by 20 % and add two new community centers in underserved neighborhoods.

The partnership was formalized during a press event held at the downtown community hall, where the nonprofit’s executive director, Maria Lopez, highlighted the role of friends in sustaining the organization’s mission. “Their commitment to our cause has allowed us to scale our services and reach more people in need,” Lopez said. City officials and local business leaders also attended the event, underscoring the broader community’s interest in supporting the nonprofit’s initiatives.

The collaboration is expected to launch in the coming month, with the first new centers slated to open by early spring. By leveraging the resources and volunteer network of its friends, Just a Little Help aims to provide more comprehensive support to families facing housing instability, food insecurity, and health challenges. The organization plans to report on the impact of the expansion in a quarterly update to its donors and community partners.
author: Space.com

title: US Government Confirms Commitment to UAP Research
content:
The newly established Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Science Advisory Council convened a private session at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) earlier this week. The meeting brought together the council’s scientific and technical experts to discuss the framework for evaluating and integrating UAP data into national security assessments.

During the session, council members reviewed preliminary findings from recent UAP investigations, outlined protocols for data sharing with defense and intelligence agencies, and identified gaps in current research capabilities. The discussion also addressed coordination mechanisms with the U.S. Department of Defense and the Federal Aviation Administration to streamline reporting and analysis of anomalous aerial events.

The council’s convening marks a formal step toward a more systematic approach to UAP phenomena. By establishing clear scientific standards and interagency collaboration, the advisory body aims to enhance the U.S. government’s ability to assess potential national security implications of unidentified aerial sightings.
author: Space.com

title: Ancestors: A Ghostly Drama on the AIDS Crisis
content:
The Toronto International Film Festival highlighted the debut feature “Saipan,” directed by David Turpin and starring Éanna Hardwicke. The film follows a soulful gay man in his twenties who embarks on a quest to locate a missing friend, weaving a narrative that blends personal longing with the broader cultural memory of the AIDS crisis. Critics noted the film’s striking visuals and its emotionally resonant, though sometimes uneven, storytelling.

Turpin, born in 1982, draws on the intergenerational trauma of the 1980s AIDS epidemic in his work. “Saipan” is his second feature, following the earlier “Ancestors,” which also tackles the legacy of the crisis through a series of vignettes. While “Ancestors” was described as intermittently impactful, “Saipan” expands on Turpin’s thematic preoccupations, exploring mortality, identity, and the enduring influence of past suffering on contemporary queer lives.

The film’s reception at the festival underscored its relevance to LGBTQ cinema, earning praise for Hardwicke’s nuanced performance and Turpin’s bold visual style. “Saipan” will continue to screen at select festivals and is slated for a limited theatrical release later this year, positioning it as a significant addition to the growing body of queer narratives that confront the historical and ongoing impacts of AIDS.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Luke Evans on Emotional Connection in ITV's The Party
content:
Actor John Doe, who portrays the troubled entrepreneur Alex Mercer in ITV’s new drama *The Party*, said in a recent interview that his “emotional connection” to the character has been a driving force behind the series. Doe explained that the role required him to navigate a complex web of ambition, regret, and redemption, and that he drew on personal experiences of ambition and loss to bring authenticity to Alex’s journey. The actor added that the intensity of the character’s internal conflict has made the filming process both challenging and deeply rewarding.

*The Party* follows Alex Mercer as he attempts to salvage his crumbling business empire while confronting the consequences of a past decision that cost him a close friend. The series, directed by acclaimed filmmaker Sarah Mills, premiered on ITV on Monday, 12 September, and is available for streaming on ITVX. Critics have praised the show for its sharp writing and strong performances, with Doe’s portrayal highlighted as a standout element of the ensemble.

The series is set to run for eight episodes, with the final instalment airing in late October. As the story unfolds, viewers will witness Alex’s struggle to reconcile his public persona with his private turmoil, a narrative that has resonated with audiences and sparked discussions about the cost of success. ITV has confirmed that *The Party* will be rebroadcast in the coming weeks, offering fans another chance to follow Alex’s emotional arc.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Oasis Confirm Knebworth Return and 2027 Live Gigs in Manchester and Glasgow
content:
The rock group **[Band Name]** confirmed a second wave of concerts for its highly anticipated reunion tour, following a series of teaser posts that had fans speculating about new dates. The announcement, released on the band’s official website and social media channels, comes after the first leg of the tour sold out within hours of ticket sales opening.

The expanded schedule adds ten additional shows across North America, including stops in Los Angeles, Chicago, Dallas, and Toronto, with dates ranging from late October through early December. Ticket sales for the new dates will begin on Friday, and the band’s ticketing partner has indicated that the venues have been selected to accommodate the high demand seen during the initial tour launch. The second wave also includes a special encore performance in New York City, a location that has historically been a fan favorite for the group.

Fans can purchase tickets through the official tour website or authorized resellers, and the band has stated that the additional dates are a response to the overwhelming demand for the reunion shows. The expanded lineup is expected to further extend the tour’s run, giving more fans the opportunity to experience the band’s classic hits live.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Hunt and Kerr Favored for BBC Sports Personality Award
content:
The BBC Sports Personality of the Year shortlist has sparked fresh debate among athletes after the recent announcement that the broadcaster will no longer publish an official shortlist. In a statement released from Budapest, British hurdler Josh Kerr cautioned that “it’s not a given, that’s the reality,” underscoring the uncertainty that now surrounds the award’s selection process. The move comes at a time when the public’s enthusiasm for athletics has surged, following a summer of high‑profile performances that have drawn widespread media attention.

The betting market has already reflected the shift in sentiment, with Amy Hunt, the Olympic 400‑metre hurdler, listed as the even‑money favourite for the title, followed by Kerr and then footballer Harry Kane. Both Hunt and Kerr have delivered standout performances in the season, making them the most likely contenders in the eyes of bookmakers and fans alike. However, the absence of an official shortlist means that athletes and their teams must now navigate a more opaque voting system, prompting concerns that the final decision could be influenced by factors beyond on‑track achievements.

As the voting deadline approaches, the BBC’s decision to keep the shortlist confidential is expected to generate further speculation about the criteria that will ultimately determine the winner. While the public remains eager to see who will receive the accolade, the athletes themselves are reminded that, despite strong odds, the outcome remains uncertain until the final vote is tallied.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Iraola Demands More Pressing from Liverpool Forwards
content:
Andoni Iraola has called for a sharper pressing effort from Liverpool’s forwards after the club’s goalless draw against Fulham. The head coach admitted that the team “took a step backwards” and that the lack of pressure up front undermined his tactical system. With the Carabao Cup tie against Tottenham Hotspur looming, Iraola has shifted the focus to the attacking line, urging them to contribute more in the high‑press phase.

Iraola noted that the midfield partnership of Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai struggled to contain Fulham’s central midfield, winning only two of five duels and one of nine respectively. He believes that the problems began further forward, where Liverpool’s expensive attacking group failed to apply the necessary pressure to force turnovers and create chances. The coach’s remarks underline a broader concern that the team’s defensive solidity is compromised when the forwards do not press aggressively.

In the lead‑up to the Carabao Cup clash with Spurs, Iraola’s emphasis on pressing will be tested. The Reds will need to combine disciplined midfield work with a more assertive forward line to avoid repeating the lackluster performance seen against Fulham. The outcome of the upcoming match will likely determine whether the tactical adjustments can translate into tangible results.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Sydney Sweeney Prediction Ad Criticized for Cynicism
content:
A recent promotional campaign by a well‑known actor has sparked widespread backlash, with critics citing the use of provocative imagery and messaging that many find offensive. The campaign, which was launched across social media platforms and television, appears to target a younger demographic, prompting calls for a boycott from several advocacy groups and a surge of negative comments on public forums.

Industry analysts suggest that the controversy may have unintended consequences for the prediction‑market sector. Prediction markets, which allow users to bet on the outcome of future events, often rely on public sentiment and media coverage to drive engagement. The actor’s campaign, by generating heightened attention and polarized discussion, could temporarily inflate trading volume and attract new participants, even as it risks alienating existing users who view the promotion as exploitative. However, the volatility associated with such high‑profile controversies also increases the likelihood of rapid price swings, potentially leading to significant losses for uninformed bettors.

While the immediate impact on the actor’s brand remains uncertain, the incident underscores the broader tension between entertainment marketing and the speculative nature of prediction markets. Stakeholders in both industries will likely monitor the situation closely, weighing the short‑term gains against the long‑term reputational risks that arise when sensationalism intersects with financial speculation.
author: Guardian Sport

title: US Solheim Cup Inquest Highlights Slow Greens, Lack of Stats
content:
A former Solheim Cup captain has warned the United States Ryder Cup team that a lack of in‑play statistical analysis could cost them on European soil. Angela Stanford, who led the U.S. side to a 15‑13 loss to Europe in the Netherlands, cited the absence of real‑time data during the match as a key factor in the defeat. She said the team’s reliance on pre‑match preparation rather than in‑play insights left them “unprepared for the pace of the competition.”

Stanford highlighted the role of data‑driven decision making by pointing to Justin Ray’s statistical contributions during the Solheim Cup. She urged Jim Furyk, who will lead the U.S. Ryder Cup team at Adare Manor next year, to adopt a similar approach. “I’m wondering how honest to be,” she said, implying that the team’s failure to use in‑play statistics was a significant oversight that could be avoided in future contests.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England approves Fleming to coach and commentate in NZ
content:
England’s new Test head coach, Stephen Fleming, will return to New Zealand in October to serve as a commentator for the Black Caps’ Test and white‑ball series against India, despite having already begun his coaching duties in England. Fleming arrived in London on Monday for a ten‑day visit that will include meetings with England captain Joe Root and the England and Wales Cricket Board’s (ECB) managing director of men’s cricket, Rob Key. The trip follows his absence from the summer’s three‑Test series against Pakistan, which the England side won 3‑0 under the guidance of batting coach Marcus Trescothick.

During his stay, Fleming will also outline plans for New Zealand’s forthcoming South Africa tour, a task he is set to tackle in the weeks ahead. The dual role of commentator and strategic planner underscores the close ties between the two cricketing boards and highlights the importance of the upcoming India series for both teams’ preparations. The arrangement allows Fleming to maintain his coaching responsibilities while contributing to New Zealand’s media coverage and tour strategy.
author: Guardian Sport

title: VARs Stood Down After Wrongly Confirming Haaland's Goal
content:
The Premier League has announced that Video Assistant Referee (VAR) officials Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus will not be assigned to any matches during the upcoming weekend. The decision follows a review of the Sunday game in which their decisions allowed Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby. Pro Ref, the governing body for match officials, confirmed that the pair have not received appointments for the round of fixtures scheduled for this weekend.

Chief Refereeing Officer Howard Webb, together with his management team, carried out the review and deemed the VAR decisions a “judgment error.” As a result, Donohue and Antrobus have been stood down pending a reassessment of their availability after the international break. The league has not yet indicated whether the officials will return to duty in the next round of matches.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Premier League title race still wide open after four games
content:
After just four league matches, pundits and fans are already debating who will finish at the top of the table. The question, raised by BBC Sport, is whether it is premature to declare a clear title race or if the standings have already narrowed to a two‑horse contest. With only a handful of points earned, the current table still shows a wide gap between the top teams and the rest of the pack, making any definitive assessment difficult.

BBC Sport’s query reflects a broader uncertainty that characterises the early stages of a football season. While a few teams may have started strongly, the small sample size of fixtures means that momentum can shift quickly. Analysts point out that early results can be misleading, and that a true title race often only crystallises after a quarter or more of the season has been played. The conversation remains open, with many experts cautioning against drawing conclusions too soon.

In the meantime, clubs will focus on building consistency rather than chasing headlines. As the season progresses, the standings are expected to become clearer, and the debate over a two‑horse race will likely settle once more fixtures have been completed. For now, the title race remains a topic of speculation rather than fact.
author: BBC Sport

title: Madrid F1 Circuit to Undergo Changes After Criticism
content:
Spanish Grand Prix organisers announced plans to modify the newly built Madrid circuit following criticism of its inaugural race weekend. The changes, aimed at improving safety and spectator experience, will focus on tightening the layout’s high‑speed sections and enhancing the pit lane configuration.

The Madrid track, unveiled last year as part of Spain’s bid to host a Formula 1 event, faced scrutiny for its narrow turns and limited runoff areas. Officials said the revisions will address these concerns while preserving the circuit’s modern design. The updated blueprint is expected to be completed before the next season’s race, ensuring the venue meets FIA standards and offers a more engaging experience for drivers and fans alike.
author: BBC Sport

title: Pollock Stays Open to New Offers During Northampton Saints Negotiations
content:
Henry Pollock, the Northampton Saints’ young lock, has entered a new phase of contract negotiations that has drawn attention from both club insiders and rival teams. The 24‑year‑old, who has become a regular starter for the Saints, is reportedly holding firm on his demands for a renewal while openly signalling that he remains receptive to offers from other Premiership clubs.

Sources say the Saints’ management are weighing the value of Pollock’s recent performances, which include a series of high‑impact line‑out wins and a growing reputation as a reliable ball‑carrier. Pollock’s representatives have highlighted his desire for a longer-term deal that reflects his contributions and future potential, yet the player has reiterated that he is not closing the door on exploring opportunities elsewhere. The club’s legal team has indicated that they are prepared to negotiate a contract that balances the player’s expectations with the team’s budgetary constraints.

With the season’s final fixtures approaching, the outcome of these talks will influence both the Saints’ squad planning and the broader transfer market. While the club hopes to secure Pollock’s services, the player’s willingness to entertain external offers keeps the negotiation dynamic, leaving fans and analysts alike to watch how the two sides ultimately resolve the matter.
author: BBC Sport

title: VAR officials Donohue and Antrobus omitted from weekend Premier League matches
content:
The Video Assistant Referee (VAR) team for the upcoming Premier League weekend will not include Matt Donohue or his assistant, Blake Antrobus. Both officials, who have served on the VAR panel for several seasons, were omitted from the list of referees assigned to the scheduled matches, including the high‑profile Manchester derby.

The decision comes as part of the league’s routine rotation of VAR personnel. While the exact replacements have not yet been announced, the Premier League confirmed that a new pair of officials will be assigned to the weekend fixtures. The change is expected to have no impact on the operation of the VAR system, which remains a key component of match adjudication.
author: BBC Sport

title: Kennedy Center board to vote on immediate building closure amid fiscal crisis
content:
The Kennedy Center’s board is scheduled to vote on Tuesday whether to shut the institution’s main building immediately for extensive renovations, a decision that comes as a court battle over renewed attempts to attach former President Donald Trump’s name to the facility continues. The proposed name change, which has faced multiple legal challenges since its initial announcement, has stalled fundraising efforts and delayed the start of a multi‑year modernization plan that the center says is essential to maintain its historic venues and technical infrastructure.

Officials warned that, without the ability to proceed with the renovation and secure new revenue streams, the performing‑arts center could experience “certain fiscal collapse within weeks,” citing mounting operating deficits and the loss of scheduled performances. The board’s vote will determine whether the center closes temporarily to address safety and code compliance issues while legal proceedings unfold, or remains open while seeking alternative financing. A closure would pause concerts, ballets and theater productions, affecting artists and audiences alike, whereas a decision to stay open could exacerbate the center’s financial strain if the naming controversy remains unresolved.
author: The Hill

title: GLP-1-driven vitamin deficiency linked to rare brain disorder: Study
content:
Researchers have identified a rare but potentially life‑threatening brain disorder in a small number of patients who were taking Ozempic, Wegovy and other glucagon‑like peptide‑1 (GLP‑1) receptor agonists. The drugs, which are approved for type 2 diabetes management and for weight loss, were linked to cases of acute neurological symptoms that progressed rapidly, prompting hospital admission and intensive care in some instances.

The study, conducted by a team of neurologists and pharmacovigilance specialists, documented a handful of patients who developed severe headaches, confusion, seizures, and in a few cases, signs of brainstem dysfunction. While the exact mechanism remains unclear, the researchers noted that the temporal association between drug initiation and symptom onset suggests a possible causal relationship. Regulatory agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration are reviewing the findings, and the manufacturers have issued a safety update urging clinicians to monitor for neurological signs in patients on these medications.

Although the incidence is extremely low relative to the millions of people prescribed GLP‑1 agonists, the discovery highlights the need for vigilance. Patients experiencing new or worsening neurological symptoms while on Ozempic, Wegovy, or similar agents should seek prompt medical evaluation. Ongoing research aims to clarify the pathophysiology and to determine whether specific risk factors predispose certain individuals to this adverse effect.
author: The Hill

title: Brothers Rescue Elderly Residents from Burning Assisted Living Facility in Glendale
content:
A blaze erupted at an assisted‑living facility on the 1800 block of Mountain Street in Glendale, California, on Friday afternoon, prompting a rapid response from the Glendale Fire Department. The fire was first reported at about 4:45 p.m., and flames quickly spread, sending heavy smoke into the surrounding neighborhood. Two young brothers, who were on the premises at the time, sprang into action and helped evacuate a group of elderly residents before the building’s fire suppression systems engaged.

Firefighters arrived within minutes and worked to contain the flames while the brothers guided the residents to safety. The facility, which houses roughly 20 residents, was fully evacuated with no injuries reported. The fire department has not yet identified a cause, and the incident is under investigation. All residents were accounted for and transported to local hospitals for routine check‑ups.

The incident underscores the importance of emergency preparedness in senior living communities. Glendale officials have pledged to review safety protocols at assisted‑living facilities and to ensure that fire suppression and evacuation plans are up to date. The city remains committed to protecting its vulnerable residents in the event of future emergencies.
author: The Hill

title: Trump meets oil refiners as analysts call for legislation to lower gas prices
content:
President Donald J. Trump met with a group of major U.S. oil refiners in Washington, D.C. to discuss plans for expanding refining capacity and boosting domestic fuel production. The meeting, held at the White House, focused on the logistics of increasing output, potential investment incentives, and the regulatory environment that could affect refinery expansion projects. Trump emphasized the administration’s commitment to supporting the industry and ensuring a stable gasoline supply for consumers.

Industry analysts, however, argue that simply expanding refining capacity will not be enough to lower gasoline prices. They point out that significant price reductions would require legislative measures to block state‑level climate lawsuits that threaten refinery operations and to counter foreign regulations that could impose stricter emissions standards on U.S. fuel. Without such policy changes, refiners warn that market forces alone may not bring the price relief many consumers are seeking.
author: The Hill

title: Bettina Trump Defends Wedding Gift From Russian Oligarch
content:
Bettina Trump, the wife of Donald Trump Jr., used her Instagram account to address rumors surrounding a wedding gift she received from Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev. In a brief post, she clarified that the couple’s nuptials were a private affair, attended only by family members, and that the gift was given in good faith.

The influencer emphasized that the wedding itself had not been a public event and that the gift, which had attracted media attention, was not intended to be a political statement. By noting the intimate nature of the ceremony, she aimed to dispel speculation that the gift was part of a larger diplomatic or financial arrangement.

Trump’s post concludes that the wedding remained a family‑only celebration, with no press or public involvement, and that the gift was simply a personal gesture from Kremlev. The clarification comes amid ongoing scrutiny of the Trump family’s relationships with foreign figures.
author: The Hill

title: DHS Report Accuses ICE of Confined Migrants at Florida Facility
content:
A new report released on Monday by the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General examined conditions at the former “Alligator Alcatraz” detention center in Florida, which was closed earlier this year. The review found that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) failed to meet a range of federal standards for the treatment of migrants, citing evidence of “unprecedented” practices. Among the most striking findings were the use of cages roughly the size of a phone booth to confine detainees, a measure that the report described as a serious deviation from established protocols for humane treatment and safety.

The investigation highlighted several areas of concern, including inadequate medical care, insufficient sanitation facilities, and a lack of adequate staffing to monitor detainees. The report also noted that the center’s infrastructure did not comply with federal guidelines for emergency preparedness and that the conditions could potentially expose detainees to health risks. ICE officials have not yet issued a formal response to the findings, but the report’s conclusions underscore the agency’s responsibility to uphold federal standards in all detention facilities.

The Department of Homeland Security has indicated that it will review the Inspector General’s recommendations and determine appropriate corrective actions. The findings may prompt further oversight and potential policy changes regarding the management of migrant detention sites across the United States.
author: The Hill

title: Jeffries to Speak on AI Safety Concerns in Press Briefing
content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D‑NY) will meet with reporters Monday afternoon to discuss growing calls for regulatory guardrails around artificial‑intelligence (AI) technology. The meeting comes after a wave of industry experts warned that the rapid pace of AI development could pose significant safety and ethical risks, prompting lawmakers to seek clearer oversight and accountability mechanisms.

Jeffries, alongside Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N‑NY), has urged the Trump administration to provide greater transparency on its plans to address these concerns. Both leaders have pressed for a coordinated federal response that would establish safety standards, data‑privacy safeguards, and a framework for monitoring AI applications in high‑stakes sectors such as finance, healthcare, and national security. The lawmakers emphasize that any regulatory approach must balance innovation with public protection.

The administration’s forthcoming policy brief is expected to outline its strategy for engaging with industry stakeholders and crafting legislation that addresses the identified risks. Lawmakers and industry observers will closely monitor the response, which could shape the U.S. regulatory landscape for AI in the coming months.
author: The Hill

title: Sydney Sweeney Criticized by Athletes Over Nude Sports Prediction Market Ad
content:
Actress Sydney Sweeney has come under fire from a growing number of female athletes after a new advertisement for the sports‑prediction market platform NoVig was released. The commercial, which features Sweeney in minimal or no clothing, opens with the actress appearing nude and asking the camera, “Think you know sports? Prove it.” The provocative imagery has sparked criticism on social media, with athletes expressing discomfort at the sexualization of a female performer in a sports‑related context.  

NoVig, a platform that allows users to bet on sports outcomes through a prediction market model, used the ad to highlight its brand’s focus on sports knowledge and betting. The choice of Sweeney—a rising star known for her roles in television and film—as the face of the campaign was intended to attract a broad audience, but the explicit content has been deemed inappropriate by many in the sports community. The backlash has led to calls for the company to reconsider its marketing strategy and for clearer guidelines on the portrayal of female talent in sports advertising.  

In response to the criticism, NoVig has not yet issued an official statement. The incident underscores the broader debate over the representation of women in sports marketing and the responsibilities of brands to maintain respectful and inclusive promotional practices.
author: The Hill

title: Kennedy Center Faces Potential Closure Amid Financial Crisis
content:
A board of trustees at a prominent arts institution released two resolutions on Monday that paint a bleak picture of the organization’s current state. The documents, now publicly available, describe the museum as being in a “dire financial and physical” condition, citing mounting debt, deferred maintenance, and a sharp decline in visitor revenue. The board’s language indicates that the institution’s survival hinges on urgent, large‑scale intervention.

In a surprising turn, the resolutions assert that only former President Donald Trump can provide the necessary rescue. The board’s statements reference the former president’s past philanthropic efforts and suggest that his involvement would secure the funding and political support required to stabilize the museum’s finances and complete critical infrastructure repairs. The claim has drawn attention from both the public and the museum’s stakeholders, who are uncertain whether the institution’s leadership is seeking a specific partnership or making a broader political statement.

The resolutions have sparked debate about the appropriate path forward for the museum. While some observers argue that the institution should pursue diversified funding sources and engage with a broader donor base, others question the feasibility of relying on a single political figure. As the museum’s trustees move forward, the outcome of this appeal to President Trump remains unclear, leaving the future of the institution in a state of uncertainty.
author: NPR Politics

title: Tice apologises for not declaring Israel trip during debate
content:
A parliamentary member’s recent trip to Israel, financed by the Reform Friends of Israel, was recorded in his register of interests but was not disclosed during the subsequent debate. The visit, which took place in late March, was funded by the pro‑Israel lobbying group that advocates for stronger ties between the UK and Israel. While the register of interests is intended to flag potential conflicts, the omission of the trip from the debate’s disclosure raised concerns about the completeness of the MP’s transparency.

The trip was listed in the MP’s official register, a document that must be updated regularly to reflect any outside funding or gifts that could influence parliamentary duties. However, when the MP spoke on the floor regarding foreign policy matters, the funding source was not mentioned. Parliamentary rules require that any relevant interests be declared at the time of debate to ensure that legislators are not unduly influenced by external parties.

The oversight has prompted calls for a review by the parliamentary ethics committee. The MP has yet to issue a statement addressing the discrepancy, and Reform Friends of Israel has not commented. The incident underscores the importance of rigorous adherence to disclosure procedures to maintain public trust in the legislative process.
author: BBC Politics

title: Former Cabinet Secretary Lord Wormald Received £860,000 Pay-off
content:
Lord Wormald, who had been appointed as the United Kingdom’s Cabinet Secretary in late 2021, stepped down in February 2023, making him the shortest‑serving holder of the post in its history.  The Cabinet Secretary is the senior civil‑service adviser to the Prime Minister and the chief executive of the Civil Service, a role that has traditionally been held for several years.  Wormald’s tenure lasted just over a year, a brief period compared with predecessors such as Sir John Manzoni, who served for more than a decade.

The decision for Wormald to leave the post came after a brief period of service that included overseeing the civil service’s response to a number of high‑profile crises and continuing reforms that had begun under his predecessor.  His departure was announced by the Prime Minister’s office as a personal choice, with no indication of a broader policy shift.  The short duration of his appointment underscores the demanding nature of the position and the high expectations placed on its occupants.
author: BBC Politics

title: UK Ministers Propose £100k Cap on Expat Donations
content:
Ministers have announced a proposal to impose a £100,000 annual cap on donations made by British expatriates, with the measure backdated to 25 March 2026. The initiative aims to standardise the contribution limits for overseas residents who support UK charities and political causes, aligning them with domestic donation thresholds.

Under the draft legislation, expatriate donors would be subject to the same financial ceiling that applies to residents, thereby preventing large, unregulated gifts from overseas. The back‑dating provision would retroactively apply the cap to any contributions received from 25 March 2026 onward, ensuring that the policy takes effect immediately for future donations while maintaining consistency with existing financial regulations.

The proposal is currently under parliamentary review, with stakeholders—including charity groups and expatriate associations—inviting comments on its potential impact. If adopted, the cap would streamline compliance for donors abroad and reinforce the integrity of the UK’s charitable funding framework.
author: BBC Politics

title: Australia Cuts Evening Gas Dependence by 70% with Battery Growth
content:
Australia’s electricity grid has seen a dramatic shift in its power mix during peak evening hours, with batteries now supplying almost half of the dispatchable capacity needed between 5 pm and 8 pm. According to a recent EnergyEdge analysis, gas‑fired generation in this critical window fell by 67% in the year to August, a decline that represents nearly 70 % of the overall reduction in gas dependence over the past year. The drop comes as large‑scale battery installations have ramped up across the country and a government subsidy program has enabled the deployment of roughly half a million home batteries.

The rapid uptake of battery storage has allowed the grid to rely less on fossil fuels when demand peaks, improving reliability and reducing emissions. While the exact mix of renewable sources feeding the batteries varies by region, the trend underscores the growing role of energy storage in meeting Australia’s peak power needs. As the grid continues to modernise, the continued expansion of battery capacity is expected to further diminish the need for gas‑based peaking plants.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Federal Court Overturns Trump Order to Keep Michigan Coal Plant Open
content:
A federal judge in Michigan dismissed the Trump administration’s attempt to keep the JH Campbell Generating plant online after its scheduled retirement, ruling that the Department of Energy had exceeded its authority. The 64‑year‑old coal‑fired facility, which the Energy Secretary Chris Wright described as essential for regional reliability, was forced to operate past its planned shutdown by invoking emergency powers. Environmental groups and the states of Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota had sued to reverse the order, arguing that the plant’s continued operation violated federal regulations and environmental standards.

The decision is part of a broader legal battle in which the administration has used emergency authority to keep several coal‑fired plants from closing. The court’s ruling underscores limits on executive power in the energy sector and signals a potential shift in how federal agencies can compel the operation of fossil‑fuel plants. The outcome may influence future disputes over the use of emergency powers to manage the nation’s aging power infrastructure.
author: Guardian Environment

title: EPA set to repeal carbon rules for coal and gas power plants
content:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is set to formally repeal the carbon‑pollution standards that limit emissions from coal‑ and gas‑fired power plants, a move that is expected to be announced on Monday during the G20 energy ministers’ meeting in Houston, Texas. Bloomberg News reported on Sunday that the decision will be made on the sidelines of the summit, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter. The repeal would undo a key component of the administration’s climate policy framework that had been in place since the Obama era.

The standards in question were designed to curb greenhouse‑gas emissions from the largest sources of electricity in the United States, requiring power plants to adopt cleaner technologies or reduce output. Critics, including environmental advocates and climate scientists, argue that the rollback effectively rewards polluters and undermines progress toward national emissions targets. The Trump administration has previously rolled back several environmental regulations, and the upcoming repeal is seen by many as the latest step in a broader trend of weakening climate safeguards.

Once the EPA formally announces the repeal, the decision will be subject to legal and political scrutiny, and it may prompt further regulatory reviews or court challenges. The move is likely to influence the trajectory of U.S. emissions policy and could affect the country’s commitments under international climate agreements.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Maryland Boy Recovering After Rabid Beaver Attack at State Park
content:
A 13‑year‑old boy from Thurmont, Maryland, is recovering after a rare attack by a rabid beaver while swimming at Cunningham Falls State Park. Dominick Cebula was submerged in the park’s popular swimming area on July 26 when the animal struck his chest underwater. He sustained severe injuries that required multiple surgeries and left him with lasting nerve damage.

Local news outlets have reported that this incident is the latest in a series of beaver‑related attacks that have occurred across the state in recent months. While beaver attacks on humans are uncommon, authorities note that the frequency of such encounters has increased, raising concerns about the spread of rabies in wildlife populations. The Maryland Department of Natural Resources is investigating the incident and reviewing safety protocols at park water sites.

Cebula’s condition is described as stable, though he remains in medical care for ongoing rehabilitation. Park officials are working with state wildlife and health agencies to assess risks and implement measures to protect visitors while monitoring the health of local beaver populations.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Reelin Protein in Lymphatic Vessels Regulates Embryonic Heart Growth
content:
A study from Northwestern Medicine has identified a previously unknown signaling system that plays a key role in regulating heart growth during embryonic development. The findings, published in the journal *Genes & Development*, reveal how this pathway orchestrates the proliferation and differentiation of cardiac cells, providing new insight into the molecular mechanisms that shape the developing heart.

Using a combination of genetic manipulation and high‑resolution imaging in mouse embryos, the researchers mapped the activity of the novel signaling cascade and demonstrated that its disruption leads to abnormal heart size and structure. The study shows that the pathway interacts with established growth regulators, such as the Hippo and Notch signaling networks, to fine‑tune cardiac cell expansion and ensure proper chamber formation. These results suggest that defects in this system could underlie certain congenital heart defects that arise during fetal development.

The discovery expands the current understanding of cardiac morphogenesis and offers a potential target for future therapeutic strategies aimed at preventing or correcting developmental heart disorders. Further research will be needed to determine how this signaling system functions in human embryos and whether it can be modulated to treat or prevent congenital heart disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Reveals Early Onset of Huntington's Disease Linked to Aggressive Symptoms
content:
A new study has identified the biological mechanisms that cause some individuals with Huntington’s disease to develop symptoms a decade or more earlier than typical and to experience a more aggressive form of the disorder. Researchers examined genetic, epigenetic, and protein‑processing differences in brain tissue from patients with early‑onset Huntington’s and found that a combination of longer CAG repeat expansions in the HTT gene, altered DNA‑methylation patterns, and increased accumulation of toxic huntingtin fragments accelerates neuronal degeneration.

The investigation, which involved both post‑mortem brain samples and advanced imaging techniques, revealed that the early‑onset group exhibited higher levels of oxidative stress markers and impaired autophagic clearance of misfolded proteins. These findings suggest that the disease’s rapid progression is driven not only by the size of the CAG repeat but also by downstream cellular pathways that fail to manage the mutant protein efficiently. The study’s authors emphasize that these insights could guide the development of targeted therapies aimed at restoring protein homeostasis and slowing disease progression in patients with severe phenotypes.

By pinpointing the molecular contributors to early onset and aggressive Huntington’s disease, the research offers a clearer framework for clinicians to identify high‑risk patients and for scientists to design interventions that address both genetic and cellular vulnerabilities. This advance marks a significant step toward personalized treatment strategies and improved prognostic tools for families affected by the disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Hydrogel Template Offers New Skin Cancer Reconstruction Option
content:
Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have announced a new method for reconstructing skin after excision of malignant lesions that could spare many patients the need for large, complex reconstructive procedures. The team’s approach employs a bioengineered scaffold that encourages the growth of the patient’s own cells, allowing the wound to heal with a more natural, integrated tissue layer.

In pre‑clinical studies, the scaffold was shown to promote rapid revascularization and collagen deposition, resulting in a robust dermal matrix that closely resembles native skin. Compared with traditional grafts or flap reconstructions, the technique reduced operative time and donor‑site morbidity, while preserving the aesthetic and functional qualities of the treated area. The researchers plan to advance the technology to early‑phase clinical trials in patients undergoing melanoma or basal‑cell carcinoma surgery.

If successful in human trials, this strategy could change the standard of care for skin‑cancer resections, offering a less invasive option that maintains both appearance and sensation. The Fox Chase team will continue to refine the scaffold’s composition and delivery method while monitoring long‑term outcomes in a broader patient cohort.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Levetiracetam May Increase Clot Risk for Patients on Blood Thinners, Study Finds
content:
Researchers from the University of Liverpool and the University of Zurich have reported a potential safety consideration linked to levetiracetam, one of the most frequently prescribed antiseizure medications worldwide. The joint investigation, which combined clinical data analysis with pharmacovigilance reporting, identified a signal that suggests an increased risk of an adverse effect in certain patient groups. Levetiracetam, commonly used to manage epilepsy and other seizure disorders, has been regarded as well‑tolerated, making the new finding notable for clinicians and regulators alike.

The study’s authors caution that the observed safety signal requires further validation through larger, prospective trials before any changes to prescribing practices can be recommended. They emphasize the importance of ongoing monitoring and suggest that healthcare providers remain vigilant for the identified risk while continuing to use levetiracetam according to current guidelines. The research adds to the broader effort to ensure the long‑term safety of widely used antiseizure therapies.
author: Medical Xpress

title: University of Iowa Study: Parents Should Pair Words with Gestures to Aid Child Learning
content:
As children return to school, a new study from the University of Iowa shows that parents can boost their kids’ learning by literally aligning with their children’s brain activity. Researchers recorded the neural signals of parents and their children simultaneously while the children performed reading and math tasks. They found that when a parent’s brain rhythms matched the child’s, the child’s comprehension and problem‑solving improved more than when the rhythms were out of sync.

The study used electroencephalography to track oscillatory activity in both brains, revealing that shared patterns of alpha and theta waves—often associated with attention and memory—were linked to better academic performance. Parents who mirrored the child’s pacing, tone, and emotional tone during instruction helped maintain this neural synchrony. The researchers suggest that simple, everyday practices—such as speaking at a similar rhythm or matching the child’s enthusiasm—can create a more conducive learning environment.

These findings point to practical strategies for families and educators alike. By fostering neural alignment, parents may help children stay focused and retain information more effectively. The University of Iowa team plans to explore how these techniques can be integrated into classroom settings and digital learning tools, potentially offering a new avenue for supporting student success.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Smartphone‑Controlled Microneedle Patch Offers Remote Pain Relief
content:
A new wearable electroceutical device has been unveiled that promises to lessen the need for hospital visits and reduce reliance on pain medication.
